contributions.headingText:
The classification of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) has been restructured to emphasize major breakthroughs over the past few years in how this disease is understood and managed. Foremost is the separation of AML with defining genetic abnormalities from AML defined by differentiation. The latter eliminates the previously confusing use of the term “AML-NOS”, under which types based on differentiation were listed. Another key change is the elimination of the 20% blast requirement for AML types with defining genetic abnormalities (with the exception of AML with BCR::ABL1 fusion and AML with CEBPA mutation). This approach was deemed more appropriate than assigning another arbitrary lower bone marrow blast cut-off point. Removal of the blast cut-off point engenders necessary correlation between morphological findings and molecular genetic studies, including the size of the clone carrying the defining genetic alteration as estimated using variant allele frequency (VAF) or fusion transcript quantitation. In future years, standardization of VAF and fusion gene calculations is anticipated to facilitate the definition of optimal lower-limit cut-off points for certain AML types with defining genetic abnormalities. A third component of the new structure is the introduction of a section on AML with other defined genetic alterations, a landing spot for new and/or uncommon AML subtypes that may (or may not) become defined types in future editions of the WHO classification. Thus, the overall AML classification structure continues to place emphasis on the integration of clinical, molecular/genetic, and pathological parameters and on clinicopathological judgement.

Although this edition retains many of the established diagnostic criteria for AML with PML::RARA, AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1, and AML with CBFB::MYH11, an increased recognition of the importance of highly sensitive techniques for evaluating measurable residual disease and of the impact of concurrent molecular alterations reflects factors that impact case management and therapeutic decisions in current practice. Namely, prognostic factors have expanded from KIT mutations, which are still relevant, to include additional cytogenetic features and measurable residual disease status after induction. The diagnostic criteria for AML with DEK::NUP214 and AML with RBM15::MRTFA (formerly RBM15::MKL1) have also remained largely unchanged.

AML with BCR::ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation are the only disease types with a defined genetic abnormality that require ≥ 20% blasts for diagnosis. The blast cut-off point requirement is needed for the former to avoid overlap with chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). Distinguishing AML with BCR::ABL1 from the initial myeloid blast phase of CML can be challenging, and additional evidence continues to be needed to better characterize this AML type. There are insufficient data to support any change in the blast cut-off criterion for AML with CEBPA mutation.

Three AML types with characteristic rearrangements involving KMT2A, MECOM, and NUP98 are recognized. A blast count under 20% is acceptable, based on studies demonstrating that patients with < 20% blasts (myelodysplastic neoplasm [MDS]) and any of these rearrangements have clinical features that resemble those with higher blast counts. It is important to note that rearrangements involving these three genes, particularly NUP98, may be cryptic on conventional karyotyping. The new term “AML with KMT2A rearrangement” replaces “AML with t(9;11)(p22;q23); KMT2A::MLLT3”. More than 80 KMT2A fusion partners have been described, with MLLT3, AFDN, ELL, and MLLT10 being the most common. Although not required, identification of the fusion partner is desirable because it could provide prognostic information and may impact disease monitoring. Adult patients often present with high blast counts, usually with monocytic differentiation. In children particularly, AML with KMT2A::MLLT3 and KMT2A::MLLT10 shows megakaryoblastic differentiation and/or low blast counts in bone marrow aspirate smears.

AML defined by mutations includes AML with NPM1 mutation and AML with CEBPA mutation. AML with NPM1 mutation can be diagnosed irrespective of the blast count, albeit again with emphasis on judicious clinicopathological correlation. This approach aligns with data showing that cases previously classified as MDS or myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm (MDS/MPN) with NPM1 progress to AML in a short period of time. Similar data have emerged from patients with clonal haematopoiesis who acquire NPM1 mutation. The definition of AML with CEBPA mutation has been changed to include biallelic mutations (biCEBPA) as well as single mutations located in the bZIP region of the gene (smbZIP-CEBPA). The favourable prognosis associated with smbZIP-CEBPA has been demonstrated in cohorts of children and adults aged up to 70 years. RUNX1 mutations in AML overlap with such a broad range of defining molecular features that it was determined they lacked enough specificity to define a standalone AML type.

Several changes were introduced to the entity formerly called AML with myelodysplasia-related changes, now called AML, myelodysplasia-related. This AML type is defined as a neoplasm with ≥ 20% blasts expressing a myeloid immunophenotype and harbouring specific cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities associated with MDS, arising de novo or after a known history of MDS or MDS/MPN. Key changes include (1) the removal of morphology alone as a diagnostic premise to make a diagnosis of myelodysplasia-related AML; (2) updated defining cytogenetic criteria; and (3) the introduction of a mutation-based definition, defined by a set of eight genes (SRSF2, SF3B1, U2AF1, ZRSR2, ASXL1, EZH2, BCOR, and STAG2), which are characteristic for AML arising after MDS or MDS/MPN.

The family of “AML defined by differentiation” includes cases that lack defining genetic abnormalities. More studies are needed to elucidate the pathogenesis of such cases, whereby the new classification scheme for AML sets the stage for better identification and characterization in the future.

The classification includes an updated comprehensive framework of differentiation markers and criteria, harmonized with those of mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia and early T-precursor lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (see appropriate sections). Indeed, the recent identification of BCL11B rearrangements in T/myeloid mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia, early T-precursor lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma, acute leukaemia of ambiguous lineage, and a subset of AML with minimal differentiation suggests a biological continuum across these entities, a finding with likely implications on future editions of the WHO classification.

Acute erythroid leukaemia (previously pure erythroid leukaemia, an acceptable related term in this edition) is a distinct AML type characterized by a neoplastic proliferation of erythroid cells with features of maturation arrest and a high prevalence of biallelic TP53 alterations. Diagnostic criteria include erythroid predominance, usually ≥ 80% of bone marrow elements, of which ≥ 30% are proerythroblasts (or pronormoblasts). The occurrence of acute erythroid leukaemia cases in which nucleated erythroid cells constitute < 80% of bone marrow cellularity is recognized. The central role that biallelic TP53 mutations play in this aggressive AML type is underscored. The diagnosis of acute erythroid leukaemia supersedes that of myelodysplasia-related AML.

Several molecular drivers can give rise to acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia, which arises within three clinical groups: children with Down syndrome, children without Down syndrome, and adults. Immunophenotyping and the detection of markers of megakaryocytic differentiation are required to make a diagnosis of acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia and detect the newly described RAM immunophenotype, which correlates with CBFA2T3::GLIS2, a subtype of AML with other defined genetic alterations.
